It was organized because members of the committee felt that the time had come to bring together those who are doing research and development in new techniques, those who operate communication networks; and the .potential customers who wish to transmit digital information. The goal was to narrow the gap between theory. and practice. As it turned out, the time was indeed propitious, and interest ran so high that the Symposium grew far larger, both in number of papers and in number of participants, than the organizing committee had originally expected. Papers were presented by authors from the USA, the United Kingdom, The Netherlands, and France, and to many it came as a pleasant surprise to find that so much work was being done in so many different places. The papers may be grouped under four headings as follows: 1) experimental results, 2) codes for error correction and detection, 3) special techniques, and 4) complete systems. Although it has not been possible to print all papers in full in this special issue of the IRE Transactions, there is given below a brief indication of the contents of each.

articleTitle: Correction [to "Some recent developments in digital feedback communication systems"]
abstract: Summary form only given, as follows. The author of the above-named work, which appeared on pages 51-57 of the March, 1961, issue of these Transactions, requested the following addition to his paper: "The research reported was performed at New York University, N.Y., under the sponsorship of the Air Force Command and Control Development Division, Air Research and Development Command, Laurence G. Hanscom Field, Bedford, Mass."

articleTitle: Meeting the challenge ahead
abstract: Our obligation as the professional group most concerned with communications systems is to help stimulate the organization of the necessary efforts, the circulation of the existing information, the definition of the problems that must be solved, and the anticipation of the equipment needs. As a necessary step in this direction we call for contributions to the organization of special issues of the TRANSACTIONS on areas of special concern. Three areas have been singled out for immediate work: Problems of Space Communication, Problems of Digital Data Transmission, and Problems of Communications Nets. Suggestions for organization of these issues and contributions in these areas are earnestly solicited. In order to secure an adequate "backbone" for each issue, special review papers are invited and will be sought from likely contributors. Coordination will be effected through the advance publication of outlines of the desired issues in this editorial section of the TRANSACTIONS. An important parting remark is in order. These special issues will not replace regular issues of the TRANSACTIONS. In order to keep up with our fundamental obligation to publish timely contributions that do not fall in these special areas, we shall publish the "special issues" as major sections of regular issues.

articleTitle: Our expanding resposibilities
abstract: As a matter of editorial policy, there will be an increased demand on contributors to present their material well. "Unreadability" is not a measure of excellence; any article whose substance cannot be grasped after two readings by an interested reader reflects badly on its writer and on the depth of his understanding of his results and their general significance and place in the field. Writers must attempt to sell their contributions, and tell the general reader right in the Introduction why their results are important or why their articles are worth reading, and at whom the presentation is beamed.

articleTitle: Why in the World in Europe?
abstract: The development of the IRE in Europe comes at a time when the European nations are busily forming ever closer ties economically, industrially, and politically. Nevertheless, although the need for better exchange of technical information within Europe is now consciously felt, it is a fact that each of the national European technical societies is handicapped by history in building a professional society for a United Europe. The IRE can build just such a society. The various IRE sections will continue to operate nearly autonomously, free to serve wherever needed and to adapt to local conditions as appropriate. They will, in the not distant future, be joined together in the structure of an IRE Region (as the Canadian sections were joined long ago). The Regional Committees, automatically both international and European, will not only help to coordinate professional-society activity, but will provide a force to attack the special problems facing the new Europe. This is the challenge facing the international IRE.
